overview.text: Multiple sclerosis (MS), also called disseminated sclerosis, is a chronic disease affecting the brain and spinal cord—the central nervous system. In MS, an abnormal immune response causes inflammation and damages myelin, the protective covering that helps nerve cells carry messages efficiently; resulting lesions can interrupt communication between the brain and body. The name “sclerosis” refers to scar tissue associated with this damage. Effects differ from person to person and may include vision problems, numbness or tingling, muscle weakness, stiffness, and balance difficulties. In relapsing-remitting MS, symptoms flare and improve or ease during remissions; progressive forms worsen gradually, either from the outset or after a relapsing course. The exact causes are not fully known, and genetic and environmental factors are thought to contribute.

key_facts.text: MS lesions affect the brain and spinal cord; MRI scans can show these damaged areas.
The three main patterns described by the NHS are relapsing-remitting, secondary progressive, and primary progressive MS.
There is no single test for diagnosing MS; assessment may include a neurological examination, MRI, blood tests, or spinal-fluid testing.
Symptoms and their effects vary; possible symptoms include fatigue, vision problems, tingling, muscle stiffness, and balance difficulties.
